title: Davy's Dazzling Arc and Ørsted's Needle
summary: A daring chemist in London used giant batteries to pull brand-new metals out of ordinary stuff and to make a light brighter than anything people had seen. Then a teacher in Denmark watched a compass needle swing beside a wire, and the world learned that electricity and magnetism are secret partners. A young bookbinder named Michael Faraday was watching it all, and he built the very first electric motor.

sections.heading: The Showman Chemist of Albemarle Street
paragraphs: Imagine pushing your way into a packed lecture hall in London in the early 1800s. Ladies in feathered hats, gentlemen in tall coats, poets, doctors and curious students squeeze onto curved wooden benches that rise steeply around a long table. On the table sit bottles, glass tubes, metal rods and rows of strange troughs full of liquid. A young man with curly hair and a quick, bright voice steps forward. Then there is a flash, a puff of smoke, and the audience gasps. This is the Royal Institution on Albemarle Street, and the man is Humphry Davy, the most exciting scientist in Britain.

Davy was born in 1778 in Penzance, a fishing town at the far south-western tip of Cornwall. He did not go to university. As a teenager he was apprenticed to a local surgeon and apothecary, a kind of chemist who mixed medicines, and he taught himself chemistry from books. He was also a keen poet and fisherman. In his early twenties he worked in Bristol, testing the effects of gases, including laughing gas, by breathing them himself, which was brave and also quite dangerous.

In 1801 the Royal Institution, a young organisation set up in 1799 to spread science and useful inventions, hired Davy as an assistant lecturer in chemistry and director of its laboratory, for 100 pounds a year. He gave his first lecture, on the new subject called galvanism, on 25 April 1801. Galvanism meant electricity made by chemical means, the kind discovered by Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta that you met in Part 4. By June 1802, aged just 23, Davy was promoted to full lecturer. His talks became so popular that they were one of the fashionable things to do in London.

What made Davy different from most chemists was one tool: the battery. Only a year after Volta announced his pile in 1800, Davy realised that a steady electric current was not just a curiosity. It was a force that could pull chemicals apart. He began building bigger and bigger batteries in the cellar of the Royal Institution, stacking hundreds and eventually thousands of metal plates in troughs of acid. In 1802 his battery was powerful enough to make a thin strip of platinum glow white-hot, an early hint of the electric light that later inventors would chase for decades. But Davy was mostly interested in something else: finding out what the world is made of.

sections.heading: Prying Metals Out of Rocks and Ashes
paragraphs: In 1800, chemists already knew many elements, the basic substances that cannot be broken down into anything simpler, such as gold, iron, sulfur and oxygen. But some common materials were puzzling. Potash, a white substance made by burning wood or plants and soaking the ashes in water, and soda, a similar substance from certain plants and minerals, were used for making soap and glass. Many chemists suspected that potash and soda contained unknown metals, but no fire, acid or chemical trick could split them.

Davy guessed that the atoms in these substances were held together by electrical attraction, so perhaps an even stronger electrical push could break them apart. This process of splitting a substance by passing an electric current through it is called electrolysis. Nicholson and Carlisle had already used it to split water into hydrogen and oxygen in 1800. Davy wanted to go further.

In the autumn of 1807 he took a lump of slightly damp potash, melted it, and passed a strong current through it from his large battery. At the negative wire, tiny shiny beads appeared, looking like drops of mercury. Some of them burst into bright flames the moment they formed. Others tarnished almost instantly, coating themselves with a white crust. Davy had found a brand-new metal, and he named it potassium, after potash. It was the first metal ever isolated by electrolysis. His cousin and assistant Edmund Davy later recalled that Humphry was so delighted that he danced about the laboratory.

Potassium is a very strange metal. It is soft enough to cut with a butter knife, it is lighter than water, and it reacts so violently with water that it fizzes, skates across the surface and catches fire with a lilac-coloured flame. That is why it had never been seen before: in nature it is always locked up tightly in compounds. Soon afterwards, using the same method on caustic soda, Davy produced another soft, silvery metal that also reacted furiously with water. He called it sodium. It is the same sodium that, joined with chlorine, makes the salt on your dinner table.

Davy did not stop there. In 1808 he reported to the Royal Society that he had isolated barium, calcium, strontium and magnesium, using electrolysis together with mercury to help collect the metals. Calcium is the element in your bones and teeth and in chalk; magnesium is the metal that burns with a blinding white light in old camera flashes and fireworks. In 1809 he isolated boron. In 1810 he showed that the green gas chemists called oxymuriatic acid contained no oxygen at all and was really an element, which he named chlorine, from the Greek word for pale green.

Think about that for a moment. In just a few years, one man with a battery in a London cellar added around half a dozen new elements to the list of known substances. Electricity had become a kind of super-tool for chemistry, able to do what fire could not. Davy became a celebrity across Europe. In 1807 the French Institute even awarded him a prize that Napoleon had set up for work on galvanism, although Britain and France were at war at the time. Davy accepted, arguing that scientists of different countries were not at war with each other.

sections.heading: A Bridge of Blinding Light
paragraphs: Davy's huge batteries had another trick. When he connected two sticks of charcoal to the ends of his battery, touched their tips together and then slowly pulled them apart, the current did not stop. Instead, it leapt across the gap as a brilliant, dazzling band of light, so bright it hurt to look at. Because his charcoal rods were held sideways, the rising hot air bent the glowing band upward into a curve like a bridge. Davy called it an arch, and the name slowly changed to arc. This was the electric arc, and the lamp made from it would be called the arc lamp.

Exactly when Davy first showed the arc is a little uncertain, and different books give dates from 1802 to 1809. He showed an early version to the Royal Society around 1806, and his most famous display came around 1808 to 1810, after the Royal Institution raised money for an enormous new battery of about 2,000 pairs of plates. With it Davy could stretch the arc across a gap of about 10 centimetres, around 4 inches. People who saw it compared it to a small piece of the Sun brought indoors.

How does an arc work? The current is so strong that it heats the tips of the carbon rods until they glow at more than 3,000 degrees Celsius, hotter than molten lava by a long way. The air in the gap becomes so hot that it starts to carry current itself, glowing as it does so. Carbon from the rods gradually turns into vapour and burns away, so the gap slowly gets wider, and someone has to keep pushing the rods closer together or the light goes out.

Davy was not the only person to find the arc. In Russia, a physicist named Vasily Petrov built an enormous battery of his own and described an electric arc between pieces of charcoal in 1803, but his work was written in Russian and was hardly known in the rest of Europe for many years. This is a pattern you will see again and again in the story of electricity: good ideas often appear in more than one place at about the same time.

Could the arc light up homes? Not a chance, at least not then. First, it was far too bright: one arc was like hundreds of candles blazing at once, perfect for a giant hall but blinding in a sitting room. Second, it hissed, flickered and sputtered, and it gave off fumes. Third, and most importantly, it was hungry. Davy's 2,000-plate battery used up its zinc and acid quickly and cost a fortune to rebuild. In 1810 there were no power stations and no generators. The arc was a magnificent show, but for the next sixty years it remained mostly a laboratory wonder. You will see arc lights finally leave the lab and light up streets, lighthouses and even a football match in Part 7.

sections.heading: The Bookbinder's Apprentice
paragraphs: Among the crowds who came to hear Davy was a young man who could not normally have afforded a ticket. His name was Michael Faraday. He was born on 22 September 1791 in Newington Butts, then a village just south of London, into a poor family. His father was a blacksmith who was often ill, and the family sometimes did not have enough bread. Michael went to school only long enough to learn reading, writing and simple arithmetic.

At the age of 14 he became an apprentice to George Riebau, a bookbinder and bookseller on Blandford Street in London. An apprentice was a young worker who learned a trade by working for a master, usually for seven years. For Faraday this was the perfect job, because he was surrounded by books all day. He did not only stitch and glue them; he read them. He was especially gripped by an article on electricity in the Encyclopaedia Britannica and by a popular book called Conversations on Chemistry by Jane Marcet, which explained chemistry through friendly discussions. He began doing small experiments of his own with whatever he could afford, building a simple electrical machine from bottles and scraps.

In 1812, near the end of his apprenticeship, a customer of the shop named William Dance gave Faraday tickets to hear Humphry Davy's lectures at the Royal Institution. Faraday sat high up in the gallery and wrote careful notes. Afterwards he copied them out neatly, added drawings of the equipment, and, being a bookbinder, bound them into a handsome volume of about 300 pages. He sent this book to Davy along with a letter asking for any job in science, however humble.

Davy was impressed, but at first he had no job to give. Then fate stepped in, in a slightly alarming way. In 1812 Davy was injured in the eye by an explosion while working with a dangerous compound called nitrogen trichloride, and for a while he could not write. Faraday helped him with his notes. Soon afterwards, a laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution was dismissed after a fight, and there was a vacancy. On 1 March 1813 Faraday was hired as Chemical Assistant, with a small wage and two rooms at the top of the building.

Only a few months later, in October 1813, Davy set off on a long tour of Europe, and he took Faraday with him as his assistant. Although Britain and France were still at war, Napoleon's government gave Davy permission to travel. For about eighteen months the young bookbinder saw Paris, the Alps and Italy, and met some of the greatest scientists of the age, including the elderly Alessandro Volta himself. It was Faraday's university. By the time they returned to London in 1815, he had learned more than any classroom could have taught him, and he was ready for the most exciting decade in the history of electricity.

sections.heading: A Needle That Would Not Sit Still
paragraphs: Now we travel north, across the sea to Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark. Here lived Hans Christian Ørsted, born in 1777 in the small town of Rudkøbing, the son of a pharmacist. He became a professor at the University of Copenhagen and was famous for his lively lectures and his love of big ideas.

For a long time, scientists treated electricity and magnetism as two quite separate things. You may remember from Part 2 that William Gilbert worked hard in 1600 to separate the magnet's pull from the amber effect. Electricity made sparks and shocks; magnetism made compass needles point north. Yet there were hints of a connection. Sailors reported that lightning strikes sometimes reversed the needles of ships' compasses, and some thinkers, including Ørsted, believed that all the forces of nature were really different faces of one deep unity. From about 1818 Ørsted was actively searching for a link between electricity and magnetism.

In the spring of 1820 he saw what he had been looking for. When a current from a battery flowed through a wire placed near a compass, the needle swung away from north. When the current stopped, the needle swung back. There is a popular story that this happened by pure accident in the middle of a lecture, but historians who have studied Ørsted's own accounts treat that as a myth. He had been looking for exactly this kind of effect, even if the result puzzled him at first. The surprising part was the direction. The needle did not point toward or away from the wire, as a magnet would be pulled toward iron. It turned sideways.

Ørsted spent the following weeks repeating the experiment with stronger batteries and trying different arrangements. He put glass, wood, water and metal between the wire and the needle, and the effect still passed straight through them. In July 1820 he published his results in a short report written in Latin, the international language of scholars, and sent copies to scientists all over Europe. It was only a few pages long, but it changed physics forever. A little later he realised what the sideways swing meant: the current creates a magnetic influence that circles around the wire, like rings around a finger.

You can picture it this way. Hold a pencil upright and imagine invisible hoops circling it at every height. If a current flows up the pencil, a tiny compass placed anywhere around it will point along those hoops. Reverse the current, and every compass flips to point the other way round. Electricity flowing in a straight line makes magnetism that goes in circles. That single fact is the starting point for electric motors, loudspeakers, doorbells, MRI scanners and electric cars.

The news spread like wildfire. Within months, scientists in Geneva, Paris, London and Berlin were all repeating the experiment. The Royal Society in London gave Ørsted its highest honour, the Copley Medal, in 1820. Today a unit of magnetic field strength used in older textbooks, the oersted, is named after him.

sections.heading: Ampère's Racing Mind
paragraphs: In September 1820 the French astronomer François Arago showed Ørsted's experiment to the Academy of Sciences in Paris. In the audience sat André-Marie Ampère, a mathematics professor born in Lyon in 1775. Ampère had had a hard life. He learned mostly from his father's library at home, and when he was a teenager his father was executed by guillotine during the French Revolution, in 1793. Ampère was known for being absent-minded and deeply thoughtful, and when he saw the swinging needle, his mind took off.

Within weeks he had made his own discoveries and presented them to the Academy. His big idea was this: if a current makes magnetism, then two wires carrying currents should push or pull on each other, even with no magnets around at all. He tested it, and he was right. Two parallel wires with currents flowing the same way attract each other. If the currents flow in opposite directions, the wires push apart. Electricity in motion behaves like magnetism.

Ampère went further. He wound wire into a long coil, which he named a solenoid, from a Greek word meaning pipe-shaped. When current flowed through it, the coil behaved just like a bar magnet, with a north end and a south end. Ampère suggested something bold: perhaps ordinary magnets are magnetic because tiny electric currents are circling inside them. He could not prove it, because nobody yet knew about electrons, but modern physics shows he was on to something important.

Most of all, Ampère turned the effect into mathematics. He worked out formulas that predicted exactly how strong the force between two currents would be, depending on how big the currents were, how far apart the wires were, and the angle between them. He called this new science electrodynamics, and he gathered it in a great memoir published in 1826. Around the same time, others found practical uses. In 1820 the German scientist Johann Schweigger wound wire many times around a compass to make the needle swing more strongly, creating an early galvanometer, an instrument for detecting and measuring current.

Decades later James Clerk Maxwell, whom you will meet in Part 6, called Ampère the Newton of electricity. In 1881 an international meeting of scientists named the unit of current the ampere, or amp for short, in his honour. Every time you read that a phone charger supplies 2 amps, you are using Ampère's name.

sections.heading: The First Electric Motor
paragraphs: Back in London, Michael Faraday had been promoted and was now doing his own research. In 1821 a friend, the editor of a science journal, asked him to write a review of everything that had been discovered about electricity and magnetism since Ørsted. Faraday, being Faraday, refused to simply copy what others said. He repeated the experiments himself, one after another.

Thinking about the circles of magnetic force around a wire, he had a brilliant idea. If the force goes round in circles, then a wire that is free to move should be pushed round and round a magnet, and never stop as long as the current flows. In early September 1821 he built a simple device to test it. He stood a bar magnet upright in a bowl and filled the bowl with mercury, a liquid metal that conducts electricity. From above, he hung a wire so that its lower end dipped into the mercury and could swing freely. Then he connected a battery so that current flowed down the wire and through the mercury.

The wire began to circle around the magnet, round and round, steadily, like a dancer twirling around a pole. In a second version, the wire was fixed and the magnet was free to move, and the magnet circled the wire. Faraday called it electromagnetic rotation. It was the first time anyone had turned electric current into continuous motion. In simple terms, it was the first electric motor. Faraday's brother-in-law later remembered him dancing around the apparatus with excitement.

It was only a toy at first. It could not lift anything or turn a wheel usefully, and it needed a dish of poisonous mercury. But it proved a principle: electricity could make things move. Every electric motor today, from the tiny one that vibrates a phone to the huge ones that drive high-speed trains, works by electric currents and magnets pushing on each other.

Sadly, the discovery also caused trouble. William Hyde Wollaston, a senior and respected scientist, had been trying to make a current-carrying wire spin on its own axis, and Davy had been involved too. When Faraday published his results without mentioning them, some people accused him of using Wollaston's ideas. Faraday was deeply upset and explained that his device worked in a different way. Wollaston himself seems to have accepted this, but the incident strained Faraday's friendship with his old master. When Faraday was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1824, Davy, by then its president, is reported to have opposed it. The bookbinder had become a rival.

sections.heading: Magnets You Can Switch On and Off
paragraphs: Ampère had shown that a coil of wire carrying current acts like a magnet. An English inventor named William Sturgeon took the next step. Sturgeon had a tough start in life: he joined the army in 1802 and taught himself mathematics and science in his spare time. Later he became a lecturer at a military college at Addiscombe, near London.

In 1824 and 1825 Sturgeon wound bare copper wire around a horseshoe-shaped piece of iron, varnished so that the wire would not touch the metal directly. When he connected a battery, the iron became a powerful magnet. His electromagnet weighed only about 7 ounces, roughly 200 grams, yet it could lift about 9 pounds, around 4 kilograms, which is about twenty times its own weight. And here was the amazing part: when he disconnected the battery, the iron lost most of its magnetism and dropped its load. Here was a magnet you could switch on and off.

Across the Atlantic, in Albany, New York, a schoolteacher named Joseph Henry made electromagnets far stronger. Sturgeon's bare wire could only be wound in one loose layer, or the turns would touch and the current would take a short cut. Henry solved this by insulating the wire, wrapping it in silk, so he could wind layer upon layer, hundreds and then thousands of turns. Starting around 1830 his magnets became astonishing. One of them, built in the early 1830s, could hold up 2,063 pounds, about 936 kilograms, which is close to a tonne, the weight of a small car.

Henry also showed that the same electromagnet could be worked from a distance, by sending current through a long wire to make a bell ring or a lever click. In 1835 he invented the electromagnetic relay, a switch worked by a small electromagnet. These were exactly the building blocks of the electric telegraph that you will meet in Part 7, and electromagnets are still everywhere today, in scrapyard cranes, electric locks, speakers and hospital scanners.

Meanwhile in Germany, a schoolteacher in Cologne named Georg Simon Ohm was asking a quieter question: how much current flows through a wire, and why? He carefully measured currents through wires of different lengths and thicknesses. In 1827 he published a book called Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet, which means The Galvanic Circuit Investigated Mathematically. In it he showed that the current in a wire depends on the push driving it, which we now call voltage, divided by how much the wire holds the current back, which we call resistance. This is Ohm's law. You will see how it works inside a light bulb in Part 11.

At first, Ohm's work was coldly received. Some German scientists thought it was too mathematical and not proper experimental science, and Ohm left his teaching job disappointed. Recognition came slowly but surely: in 1841 the Royal Society in London gave him the Copley Medal, and the unit of resistance, the ohm, is named after him.

By 1827, then, the world had learned a huge amount in just a few years. A current could split chemicals, make dazzling light, swing a compass, attract another wire, spin a wire around a magnet and turn a lump of iron into a crane. Electricity could make magnetism. And Michael Faraday, scribbling in his notebook at the Royal Institution, could not stop thinking about one question. If electricity can make magnetism, can magnetism make electricity?

deepDive: Why was Ørsted's result so shocking to physicists in 1820? Every force known before it, such as gravity and the pull between electric charges, acts along the straight line joining two objects. Ørsted's needle did something new: the force from the current pointed sideways, around the wire. Today we describe this with the idea of a magnetic field whose lines form closed circles around a current. The strength of that field falls off with distance, roughly in proportion to 1 divided by the distance from a long straight wire, which Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart measured in Paris in 1820. Ampère's achievement was to write the force between two current-carrying circuits as a mathematical law, and his work later became the basis of the official definition of the ampere: for most of the twentieth century, one ampere was defined as the current that, flowing in two thin parallel wires one metre apart, produces a force of 2 × 10^-7 newtons per metre of length between them. (Since 2019 the ampere has been defined instead by fixing the charge of a single electron.) Historians also debate how to share credit for the motor. Faraday's 1821 rotation device turned current into continuous motion, but it was weak and needed mercury. In 1822 Peter Barlow built a spinning star-shaped wheel dipping into mercury, and in 1832 William Sturgeon showed a motor with a commutator, a rotating switch that reverses the current at just the right moment so the motor keeps turning in one direction. Practical motors grew from all these steps. Davy's arc raises another debate: he is often named its discoverer, yet Vasily Petrov described a continuous arc in 1803 and the dates of Davy's own early demonstrations are uncertain. A sensible conclusion is that the arc was found independently by several experimenters once batteries became large enough. Finally, Ohm's law looks simple, V = I × R, but in 1827 it was hard to test, because batteries of the time gave voltages that drifted as they were used. Ohm's careful measurements were part of what made his result convincing in the end.
funFact: Potassium, the metal Humphry Davy discovered with his battery in 1807, is so soft you could cut it with a butter knife, and it reacts so strongly with water that it bursts into a lilac-coloured flame.

check.q: What did Hans Christian Ørsted see in 1820 that showed electricity and magnetism are linked?
check.a: A compass needle swung when an electric current flowed through a nearby wire
wrong: A frog's leg twitched when touched with two metals
A kite collected sparks from a storm cloud
A copper disc made electricity when it spun between magnets
